capture.final_message:
Split the conjunction.

For the first statement, view both linear equivalences as the same map induced by the identity on \(M\). Use extensionality for linear equivalences, followed by quotient induction: on every representative \(m\), both maps send \([m]_P\) to \([m]_Q\). Any difference in the proof terms used to show \(P=Q\) disappears by proof irrelevance.

For the second statement, use the quotient projection
\[
\pi : M_2 \to M_2/\operatorname{range}(f).
\]
Compare \(u=\pi\) with \(v=0\). Since every \(f(m)\) lies in \(\operatorname{range}(f)\), both composites with \(f\) are zero. The assumed cancellation property therefore gives \(\pi=0\). Hence every \(x\in M_2\) has zero quotient class, which by the kernel characterization of the quotient projection means \(x\in\operatorname{range}(f)\). Thus every element belongs to the range, so \(\operatorname{range}(f)=\top\).

The main mechanism is therefore quotient extensionality in the first component and the fact that the quotient projection has kernel exactly \(\operatorname{range}(f)\) in the second.
